justification: Checklist interviews with group representatives (surveys), FGDs (participatory), satellite imagery (remote sensing) and field observation/cited census data are all used. B omits the interviews. A slightly over-codes secondary_data.
A reproduces the authors' recommendations (respect farmers' initiatives, seek adaptations within local culture, longitudinal studies). B largely restates findings.

No group is targeted or has results disaggregated; women appear only in a membership table, and youth and ethnic minority are never addressed (Matengo is the local ethnic group, not framed as a minority). none_reported is correct.

Checklist interviews, FGDs and content analysis make this qualitative. Participatory is not the primary design, so A over-codes it; quantitative is only weakly supported by the satellite land-cover tables.

The paper reports group formation (participation), adoption of strategies, hydro-mill revenues and savings/loans (income, credit access), umbrella committees (governance) and livelihood diversification. Decision-making and knowledge are not measured.

Crops, livestock, fish farming and tree planting/agroforestry are all practised and reported as separate activities; 'mixed' is reserved for explicitly mixed crop-livestock systems and omits fish and trees.
Springer book chapter published 2012; B's 'none' is not a valid year.
The authors state only one limitation (preliminary study). B's strength is the coder's own description of methods, not an author appraisal.
The paper uses 55 structured interviews, PLA tools, instrument and soil measurements (other) and cited surveys/census data (secondary). B omits most of these.
A states the authors' recommendations (involve farmers from the outset, monthly hands-on workshops). B is mostly findings.
Women are disaggregated (separate women's and men's matrix scoring, interpreted by gender). Youth is not targeted or disaggregated.
Farmer-managed trials with control beds and instrumented water balance are on-farm experiments, which the rules count as experimental, alongside participatory (PLA) and survey elements.

Decision-making, learning, adoption, participation in workshops/groups and food security are the measured themes. Institutional governance is not examined and income is not a measured outcome of the practices.
The study concerns homestead vegetable gardens and crops; livestock appears only as context (free-roaming animals), not as a studied system, so mixed is not supported.

A matches the authors' own appraisal: small, unrepresentative sample, poorest missed, less-controlled trials, and good-quality data. B reports findings about drip kits and facilitation, not self-appraisal.
Case studies ran for 9 months within one agricultural year, which the tie-break classes as seasonal. The follow-up statements are anecdotal rather than repeated measurement across years.
B captures the authors' main policy recommendations plus future research; A quotes only the future-research sentences and omits the principal recommendations.
A semi-structured questionnaire analysed with Heckman and beta regression is purely quantitative; no qualitative analysis is reported.

Determinants of diversification (adoption) include credit, extension and information sources (access), and outcomes are income share and livelihood diversification. Knowledge and participation are not outcomes measured.

The study is of cocoa (a tree crop) farmers; livestock rearing is a measured diversification strategy, so crop alone (A) or crop; livestock (B) are defensible. Agroforestry in B is not stated by the authors.
The study uses interviews with 60 collectors, FGDs, GMet climate data and secondary reviews, plus a field environmental threat assessment. B covers these; A omits most.
Three neighbouring communities were sampled, so the multi-village rule gives sub-national; local is for a single site. A single-estuary framing makes local arguable but weaker.
Results are disaggregated by gender (women versus men) and interpreted. Youth are not addressed; the sample was selected as aged 40 and above.
The authors describe a triangulation using participatory tools, but the design is interviews, FGDs and ranking statistics, not PRA as primary design; both codings are defensible.

The paper measures perceptions/indigenous knowledge of climate variability, adoption of adaptation strategies, constraints (information, markets) and livelihood diversification. Income is not measured.
The authors give no appraisal of their own study. A's strength is just the paper's aim, and its format is unusable.
Data come solely from focus groups, i.e. participatory_methods; A contains invalid or misspelled values and surveys is unsupported.
Focus groups were held around several communities in Haiti's mountain areas, a sub-national scale; A is not a valid single code.
Men and women were interviewed separately and results reported gender by gender. 'men' is not a valid code and youth is not disaggregated, so women only.
Focus-group data analysed by the constant comparative method is qualitative; A adds invalid values.
B uses valid codes consistent with the themes (information access, decision-making, perceptions, coping behaviour, yield changes). A is free text and invalid.
Crop and livestock production and risks are discussed as separate systems, which fits 'crop; livestock' rather than an explicitly integrated mixed system.
A reproduces the authors' Limitations paragraph. B adds limitations the authors do not state (cross-sectional, no cost data, social desirability) and is malformed.

The paper uses 20 FGDs and interviews (participatory_methods), MODIS NDVI (remote_sensing), Xinjiang Statistical Yearbook yield data (administrative_data) and meteorological station records (secondary_data). A omits these.
Taxkorgan is a county (25,000 km2) with multiple sites and 20 focus groups across communities; it is a district-level unit within China, so sub-national, not a single local site.

A states recommendations (incorporate crop-climate model findings into calendars, with field corroboration, water management). B restates a finding about warming and crop maturation, not a recommendation.

Design is interviews/FGDs (qualitative) plus PLS regression of yield on climate indices (quantitative). PLS is statistical regression and is not a validated simulation model; participatory action research is mentioned but is not the primary design.

Crop yield is the regressed outcome (yields_productivity), changes in sowing dates are documented (behavioral_change), and local ecological knowledge and calendar-based decisions are reported. No resilience or adaptive-capacity index is measured, so A's resilience_adaptive_capacity is unsupported and A omits yields.

A uses the authors' own appraisal: results applicable at farm level, need for in-field corroboration, and discontinuous barley data. B's strength (integrating records, remote sensing and ethnoecological knowledge) is a description, not an author-stated strength.
Only primary survey data are analysed. Department of Agriculture registration statistics were used just to draw the sampling frame, so administrative_data is not a data source.

A states the authors' recommendations (scale up adaptation, continuous extension training, subsidised improved seed). B opens with a finding (negative climate impact on yield and income) and runs items together.
No group is targeted or has results disaggregated; age appears only as a descriptive variable, so youth is not supported.
Structured questionnaire analysed with descriptive statistics and paired t-tests only; nothing qualitative.

The paper measures maize output (yields_productivity), income (income_assets), adaptation strategy use (uptake_adoption) and constraints such as extension, credit and information access (access_information_services). B omits yield and adds behavioral_change, decision_making, knowledge and wellbeing, which are not measured.

The authors do evaluate their instrument (very reliable, r = 0.86) and their sampling design, which counts as a stated strength. No limitations are given, so B's strength-only content is more faithful than A's blanket 'not reported'.
A single survey was conducted in January-April 2022; recall of the last two seasons does not make it longitudinal under the project rule that the study's own data collection design governs.

Questionnaire survey of 293 farmers plus SPI/SDI computed from existing rain-gauge and streamflow records; under the project rule, meteorological station records are secondary_data, not administrative data.

B gives recommendations (multi-level governance, stakeholder engagement, reliable data, evaluating costs of action versus inaction). A mixes in findings (rain-fed farming raises vulnerability) and statements about forecast benefits that the paper does not test.

The vulnerability index includes adaptive capacity (resilience_adaptive_capacity), adoption of practices such as new varieties, tillage and sowing date changes (uptake_adoption), and use of forecasts, extension contact and credit (access_information_services). B's behavioral_change, decision_making, institutional_governance and knowledge are not measured.

The authors claim novelty as a strength but give no limitations of their own study. A's 'limitations' (weak governance, data poverty in Iran) describe the national DEWS context, not the study's own limits.
The farmer questionnaire was a single cross-section; the 30-year climate series is secondary hazard input, not the study's own repeated data collection.
Age is a regressor and descriptive category only; youth are not targeted and outcomes are not disaggregated by youth. Small subsistence farmers are a landholding class, not a listed group.

The outcome is the decision to purchase insurance, with access to credit, extension and information and risk perception as variables. Income is only a regressor (average monthly income), not an outcome, so A's income_assets is over-inclusion.
A uses authors' own appraisal: findings applicable to other developing regions, limited to four districts, needs replication. B's 'strength' is the main finding, not an appraisal of the study.

About 365 household questionnaires (surveys), FGD/PRA (participatory_methods), Landsat (remote_sensing), literature and FAO data (secondary_data), plus soil lab analysis and tree inventory (other). B omits the central household survey.

B reproduces the authors' explicit 'Lessons learnt' section (partnership building took longer than expected, short timelines and contract delays). A reproduces the authors' technical recommendations (fertilizer trees, micro-dosing, Climate Field Schools). Both are author recommendations; B is closer to the labelled lessons.

Women are discussed explicitly: sex-specific adaptation strategies and fuelwood collection roles are reported. Youth appear only in age breakdowns and a general call to motivate young people, not as a targeted or disaggregated group.

Core design is a structured household survey with descriptive statistics, plus soil analysis, remote sensing and literature synthesis. PRA and mapping are used but participation is not the primary design under the codebook, so 'participatory' is a stretch (B is defensible but weaker).

The baseline measures income, food security months, fertilizer and seed use, access to improved seed and weather information, awareness of tree benefits, yields and policy environment. B's participation_coproduction (PRA is a method) and risk_reduction are not measured outcomes.

The project evaluates Evergreen Agriculture, an agroforestry model (tree inventories, tree seed supply) in maize-mixed and agro-pastoral crop-livestock systems. Agroforestry is central, so B is more complete.

The authors report deviations (short project, late start, site change, 600 of 1000 farmers reached) as limitations but do not appraise any strength of their own design. A's strength (partner integration, co-location) is a description of partnerships and a site change, not an author-stated strength.
Paper reports explicit premium costs per TLU (KES487-825), subsidy percentages and payout amounts (KES3,235): explicit cost figures for the intervention. B's 'no' ignores these.
B captures the authors' main practical recommendations (promote uptake/scaling, enabling environment given low adoption) plus research needs; A covers only future-research suggestions.
2SLS-IV using randomly assigned subsidy coupons for causal identification counts as experimental under the coder brief; there is no qualitative component, only household panel surveys.
Outcomes are household income, income variance/skewness (downside risk) and IBLI uptake; 'access_information_services' alone misses all of these.
Study population is pastoralist/agropastoralist livestock keepers and the insured asset is livestock; no explicit mixed crop-livestock system is analysed, so adding 'mixed' is unsupported.

A reflects author statements (first evidence from a livestock setting; Hansen J caveat on instrument exogeneity). B pastes policy-implication text, not an appraisal of the study, and reports no limitation although authors note the Hansen J caveat.

B reflects the authors' recommendations (water user organisations, watershed committees, cooperatives, integrate into CRGE, invest in extension/infrastructure). A only states that policy implications are generated.

Sex of household head is a regressor with a significant coefficient for one strategy and brief gender remarks, but there is no targeting or real gender-disaggregated analysis; both readings are defensible.

Study analyses determinants of adoption of five water adaptation strategies (uptake_adoption), with extension/media/networks (access_information) and perception of climate impacts (knowledge). Income is only a covariate and decision-making is not separately measured, so A over-codes income_assets/decision_making.
Authors describe 'a mixed farming agricultural system' but list almost only crops; crop is defensible, mixed is defensible on the authors' wording.

B reflects the authors' own claim of methodological innovation/robustness of the MVP; A's quote is a generic statement of contribution about water resources, not an appraisal of design. Neither has an author limitation.
Household survey, 12 FGDs and 15 key-informant interviews were used: surveys and participatory_methods. A's 'un_clear' is not a valid code and the sources are clear.
Three districts across Uganda's cattle corridor is sub-national; 'local' means a single site and multi-value entry is not allowed.

B reflects the authors' Recommendations section (integrate gender-responsive strategies into national plans, invest in adaptation, reform financial institutions, credit/inputs considering gender). A restates findings.
Women are the explicit gender focus with disaggregated results. B adds men, adults, elders, which are not valid marginalised codes (men and adults are not marginalised groups).

Study measures adopted strategies, changes in incomes, assets/social capital and household welfare, and livelihood diversification, so income_assets, livelihoods, uptake_adoption, wellbeing fit. A's decision-making, risk-reduction and resilience codes are not measured outcomes (and are invalid strings).
Households are agro-pastoralists with both crop and livestock strategies. 'mixed' and 'crop; livestock' (B's malformed entry, same substance) are both defensible.

A gives an author-stated strength (sample surpassing minimum, bolstering validity) and limitation (strategies explain only ~33%, other factors may matter). B is garbled, describes study focus rather than an appraisal, and asserts no visible limitation.
Authors state a cross-sectional design; 'un_clear' is incorrect.
Survey covers six counties of Yulin City (one prefecture), i.e. sub-national, not the whole of China.

B accurately renders the authors' recommendations (subsidies/training for non-adopters, cost-sharing, adopters as secondary disseminators, recovery of plastic mulch and drip tape). A is thinner and includes a finding.
No marginalised group is targeted or disaggregated; 'small_holder_farmers' is not a valid code and smallholder is the population, not a marginalised subgroup.

Study examines intention to adopt/promote/pay for WSI as a function of policy evaluation and perceptions: uptake_adoption, institutional_governance (policy evaluation) and decision_making fit. A's resilience_adaptive_capacity is not measured.

B follows the authors' stated gap-filling and endogeneity-test strength and their stated limitations (questionnaire data, narrow scope, few factors, endogeneity testing not exhaustive). A mixes in items the authors do not claim as strengths (large sample, TAM-SEM).
Journal of Agricultural Extension Vol. 27(2), published 2 April 2023; 2022 was only the submission year.
